thread.title: HP sticks with successful strategy in new lineup of premium PCs - MarketWatch

author: Emily Bary
title: HP sticks with successful strategy in new lineup of premium PCs - MarketWatch
text:
Despite slow growth in the personal-computer industry and high component costs, HP Inc. has found ways to flourish.
The computer manufacturer has thrived amid tough industry conditions thanks to a focus on premium PCs , which has allowed the company to c ommand higher prices for its devices at a time when rivals are betting on the low-end market. HP HPQ, -0.18% continued that push on Monday, when it announced a number of new premium models across its consumer and commercial segments.
Some, like upgraded versions of the EliteBook x360 1030 notebook and the Elite x2 1013 business detachable, cost incrementally more than their predecessors. These two models, which are on the commercial side, feature enhancements meant to appeal to enterprise customers whose employees do work outside the office.
The x360, for example, has built-in 4G LTE and anti-glare etching, and the X2 1013 has a privacy screen built in, which HP claimed in a media briefing last week was a first for the detachable category. While the x2 1013 doesn’t look as cool as an iPad Pro, its detachable keyboard has considerable “travel,” meaning you can feel yourself push the keys down. It’s a serious device that has appeal for those doing work on the go.
See also: HP reclaims top spot in PCs, but staying there isn’t the top priority
Mike Nash, HP’s head of portfolio strategy, told MarketWatch that before HP began emphasizing premium models on the corporate side, companies didn’t see much distinction between HP’s two categories of computers and would end up buying consumer models for their employees. That was bad for HP’s business. According to Nash, it also meant that employees ended up bringing their home computers to work because they didn’t like what their company provided, which posed a security risk.
He believes that HP has made progress over the past three years with its introduction of enterprise devices that consumers feel are “as good as” their home computers. “The feedback we hear from the millennial subsegment is that they’re going to pick the company they work for based on a number of different things,” Nash said, and one of them is “what tech do I get?”
Across its consumer and commercial divisions, HP unveiled 11 new products or models Monday. The company’s sprawling portfolio, which extends beyond the devices announced this week, stands in contrast to that of Apple Inc. AAPL, -0.38% which essentially has three laptop models and three desktop ones. Nash argued that HP has more demand curves to satisfy than Apple.
“When you sell things to enterprise customers, they don’t want things to change every year, and they want things design-wise to be much more consistent,” Nash said. Consumers, meanwhile, might not want to pay extra for devices that are compatible with docking stations from years ago, durable enough to get bounced around in an overhead compartment, or impervious to onlookers via a privacy screen.
Don’t miss: Apple education event shows company hasn’t learned its lesson
Of course, the vast array of products for both consumers and enterprises means HP has more work to do in terms of making sure that people end up choosing the right one.
On the consumer side, the company announced a new “super premium” Envy 13 laptop with “drop chin” technology that essentially angles the keyboard once the computer is opened, giving the fan more air at the bottom. HP also rolled out a new 15-inch Envy X360 laptop with a keypad on the side, which Nash said was popular on the previous model.
HP’s focus on premium has proven a winning strategy lately, with shares up 18% over the past 12 months, while the S&P 500 index SPX, +0.17% has gained 14%.
